claim: Burst spiking in substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) dopaminergic neurons is a key signaling event in the circuitry controlling goal-directed behavior.
source: Burst spiking in substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) dopaminergic neurons is a key signaling event in the circuitry controlling goal-directed behavior.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that draws on established scientific knowledge about SNc dopaminergic neurons and their role in behavior.

claim: It is widely believed that burst spiking in SNc dopaminergic neurons depends upon an interaction between synaptic activation of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs) and intrinsic oscillatory mechanisms.
source: It is widely believed that this spiking mode depends upon an interaction between synaptic activation of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs) and intrinsic oscillatory mechanisms.
evidence: This statement references the prevailing view in the field, drawing on established scientific consensus.

claim: PPN glutamatergic synapses on SNc dopaminergic neurons are localized exclusively on the soma and proximal dendrites.
source: These synapses were localized exclusively on the soma and proximal dendrites, placing them in a good location to influence spike generation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from sCRACM mapping experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Burst stimulation of PPN axons was faithfully followed even in the presence of NMDAR antagonists.
source: Moreover, burst stimulation of PPN axons was faithfully followed, even in the presence of NMDAR antagonists.
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: PPN-evoked burst spiking of SNc dopaminergic neurons in vivo may be extrinsically triggered and extrinsically patterned.
source: Thus, PPN-evoked burst spiking of SNc dopaminergic neurons in vivo may not only be extrinsically triggered, but extrinsically patterned as well.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing AMPAR-dependent burst generation.

claim: SNc dopaminergic neurons play a central role in modulating goal directed actions and habits under the control of the basal ganglia.
source: SNc dopaminergic (DA) neurons play a central role in modulating goal directed actions and habits, which are under the control of the basal ganglia.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of neuroscience.

claim: The spiking behavior of SNc DA neurons can be placed into two broad categories: a single spiking, low-frequency (<10 Hz) mode and a multi-spike, higher frequency, 'burst' mode.
source: The spiking behavior of these cells can be placed into one of two broad categories – a single spiking, low-frequency (<10 Hz) mode and a multi-spike, higher frequency, 'burst' mode (Grace and Bunney, 1984a, 1984b; Hyland et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by Grace and Bunney (1984a, 1984b) and Hyland et al. (2002).

claim: The single spiking mode is critical for maintaining ambient levels of DA in target structures.
source: The single spiking mode is critical for maintaining ambient levels of DA in target structures, while the burst mode is thought to be a fundamental signal for action selection and reward-based learning (Schultz, 2007, 2016; Tsai et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schultz (2007, 2016) and Tsai et al. (2009).

claim: The burst mode is thought to be a fundamental signal for action selection and reward-based learning.
source: The single spiking mode is critical for maintaining ambient levels of DA in target structures, while the burst mode is thought to be a fundamental signal for action selection and reward-based learning (Schultz, 2007, 2016; Tsai et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schultz (2007, 2016) and Tsai et al. (2009).

claim: The single spiking mode of SNc neurons is generated by an intrinsic pacemaking mechanism involving the cooperation of Na+, K+, and Ca2+ ion channels.
source: The single spiking mode of SNc neurons is generated by an intrinsic pacemaking mechanism involving the cooperation of a number of Na+, K+, and Ca2+ ion channels (Shepard and Bunney, 1988; Nedergaard et al., 1993; Chan et al., 2007; Puopolo et al., 2007; Guzman et al., 2009; Ding et al., 2011; Kimm et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Single spiking behavior is preserved in the absence of synaptic input and is observed in both dissociated and ex vivo brain slice preparations.
source: This behavior is preserved in the absence of synaptic input, and is observed in both dissociated and ex vivo brain slice preparations (Chan et al., 2007; Puopolo et al., 2007; Guzman et al., 2009; Ding et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Burst spiking is lost in preparations lacking functionally intact synaptic connectivity.
source: In contrast, burst spiking is lost in preparations lacking functionally intact synaptic connectivity (Shepard and Bunney, 1991; Johnson and Wu, 2004; Blythe et al., 2007) and is disrupted in vivo by local application of glutamatergic receptor antagonists (Grace and Bunney, 1984b; Charlety et al., 1991; Overton and Clark, 1992; Smith and Grace, 1992; Chergui et al., 1993), demonstrating the necessity of synaptic activity for the production of these events.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Burst spiking is disrupted in vivo by local application of glutamatergic receptor antagonists, demonstrating the necessity of synaptic activity for burst generation.
source: In contrast, burst spiking is lost in preparations lacking functionally intact synaptic connectivity (Shepard and Bunney, 1991; Johnson and Wu, 2004; Blythe et al., 2007) and is disrupted in vivo by local application of glutamatergic receptor antagonists (Grace and Bunney, 1984b; Charlety et al., 1991; Overton and Clark, 1992; Smith and Grace, 1992; Chergui et al., 1993), demonstrating the necessity of synaptic activity for the production of these events.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple in vivo studies.

claim: Local infusion of NMDAR antagonists in vivo reduced burst activity in anesthetized rodents.
source: Because local infusion of NMDAR antagonists in vivo reduced burst activity in anesthetized rodents (Overton and Clark, 1992; Chergui et al., 1993), subsequent studies have focused on the potential mechanisms by which NMDARs might generate naturally occurring bursts.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Overton and Clark (1992) and Chergui et al. (1993).

claim: NMDARs can amplify intrinsic oscillatory activity and promote the transition from slow, single spike pacemaking to a burst pattern.
source: Indeed, NMDARs can amplify intrinsic oscillatory activity and promote the transition from slow, single spike pacemaking to a burst pattern (Wilson and Callaway, 2000; Kuznetsov et al., 2006; Deister et al., 2009; Kuznetsova et al., 2010; Ha and Kuznetsov, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: AMPARs appear unable to produce burst activity like that observed in vivo.
source: In contrast, α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) receptors (AMPARs), the other ionotropic glutamate receptor found at SNc glutamatergic synapses, appear unable to produce burst activity like that observed in vivo (Shepard and Bunney, 1991; Johnson and Wu, 2004; Deister et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Local electrical stimulation of glutamatergic axons can induce burst-like spiking in SNc DA neurons that is dependent upon AMPARs.
source: However, local electrical stimulation of glutamatergic axons can induce burst-like spiking in SNc DA neurons that is dependent upon AMPARs (Georges and Aston-Jones, 2002; Blythe et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Georges and Aston-Jones (2002) and Blythe et al. (2007).

claim: Rabies virus tracing studies have identified glutamatergic neurons in the subthalamic nucleus (STN), cerebral cortex, superior colliculus, and pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN) that synapse on SNc DA neurons.
source: Rabies virus tracing studies have identified a handful of glutamatergic neurons that synapse on SNc DA neurons, including those in the subthalamic nucleus (STN), cerebral cortex, the superior colliculus and the pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN) (Watabe-Uchida et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Watabe-Uchida et al. (2012).

claim: The PPN is of particular interest because of the strength of its projection to SNc and its connectivity with the rest of the basal ganglia.
source: Of these, the PPN is of particular interest because of the strength of its projection to SNc and its connectivity with the rest of the basal ganglia (Clarke et al., 1987; Lavoie and Parent, 1994a, 1994b; Charara et al., 1996; Mena-Segovia et al., 2004; Martinez-Gonzalez et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple anatomical studies.

claim: PPN neurons respond to environmental events in a way that resembles SNc DA neurons, including burst spiking in response to salient and rewarding stimuli, but at latencies shorter than those observed in DA neurons.
source: Interestingly, PPN neurons respond to environmental events in a way that resembles SNc DA neurons, including burst spiking in response to salient and rewarding stimuli, but at latencies shorter than those observed in DA neurons (Condé et al., 1998; Kobayashi et al., 2002; Pan and Hyland, 2005; Norton et al., 2011; Thompson and Felsen, 2013; Hong and Hikosaka, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple in vivo recording studies.

claim: Activation of the PPN in vivo can evoke repetitive spiking in SNc DA neurons.
source: Moreover, activation of the PPN in vivo can evoke repetitive spiking in SNc DA neurons (Scarnati et al., 1984; Lokwan et al., 1999; Floresco et al., 2003; Hong and Hikosaka, 2014), and ablation of the PPN disrupts learning operant tasks (Inglis et al., 2000; Wilson et al., 2009; Bortolanza et al., 2010; Syed et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple in vivo studies.

claim: Ablation of the PPN disrupts learning operant tasks.
source: Moreover, activation of the PPN in vivo can evoke repetitive spiking in SNc DA neurons (Scarnati et al., 1984; Lokwan et al., 1999; Floresco et al., 2003; Hong and Hikosaka, 2014), and ablation of the PPN disrupts learning operant tasks (Inglis et al., 2000; Wilson et al., 2009; Bortolanza et al., 2010; Syed et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple behavioral studies.

claim: Injections of AAV9 ChR2-eYFP driven by the human Synapsin I promoter were made into the PPN of wild-type or DAT-Cre/Ai14-tdTomato mice.
source: Injections of adeno-associated virus serotype 9 (AAV9) ChR2-eYFP driven by the human Synapsin I (hSyn) promoter were made in to the PPN of wild-type or DAT-Cre/Ai14-tdTomato mice (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used, as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Projections from the PPN to SNc were visualized ten days after injection.
source: Projections from the PPN to SNc were visualized ten days after injection (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This is supported by the images shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Photo-stimulation of ChR2-expressing PPN cells with full-field blue light LED illumination reliably evoked photocurrents and associated action potentials.
source: Photo-stimulation of these cells with full-field (~360 µm diameter) blue light (473 nm) LED illumination reliably evoked photocurrents and associated action potentials (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: Paired-pulse stimulation (20 Hz) evoked responses with amplitude ratios less than one, indicating that the PPN glutamatergic synapse had a high release probability.
source: Paired-pulse stimulation (20 Hz) evoked responses with amplitude ratios less than one (Figure 1E; PPR = 0.83 ± 0.13, n = 10), indicating that the PPN glutamatergic synapse had a high release probability.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the paired-pulse ratio data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The NMDAR current at PPN synapses was roughly half that of the AMPAR current.
source: Measured in this way, the NMDAR current was roughly half that of the AMPAR current (peak AMPAR current/peak NMDAR current = 1.43 ± 0.42, n = 13).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the AMPA:NMDA ratio data.

claim: At PPN synapses on SNc dopaminergic neurons, there was no discernible rectification at depolarized membrane potentials, suggesting AMPARs at this synapse had edited GluA2 subunits.
source: At PPN synapses on SNc dopaminergic neurons, there was no discernible rectification at depolarized membrane potentials (Figure 2A), suggesting AMPARs at this synapse had edited GluA2 subunits.
evidence: This is supported by the current-voltage relationship data shown in Figure 2A and draws on established knowledge about GluA2-containing AMPARs.

claim: The polyamine toxin philanthotoxin-74 failed to significantly reduce the AMPAR currents at PPN synapses, indicating the presence of the GluA2 receptor subunit.
source: Furthermore, the polyamine toxin philanthotoxin-74, which preferentially antagonizes GluA2-lacking (GluA1 and GluA3 homomeric) AMPARs (Poulsen et al., 2014), failed to significantly reduce the AMPAR currents (Figure 2B), again indicating the presence of the GluA2 receptor subunit.
evidence: This is supported by the pharmacological data shown in Figure 2B and citation to Poulsen et al. (2014).

claim: The GluN2A-selective antagonist TCN 201 had no effect on NMDAR currents at PPN synapses (7.76 ± 18.40%, n = 6, p=0.4375).
source: In contrast, the GluN2A specific antagonist TCN 201 (Edman et al., 2012) had no effect on NMDAR currents (Figure 2C–D; % change: 7.76 ± 18.40, n = 6, p=0.4375).
evidence: This is supported by the pharmacological data shown in Figure 2C-D and citation to Edman et al. (2012).

claim: NMDARs at PPN synapses contain GluN2B and GluN2D subunits.
source: In agreement with previous work, both the GluN2B specific antagonist ifenprodil (Williams, 1993) and the GluN2C/D specific potentiator CIQ (Mullasseril et al., 2010) altered the amplitude of the evoked NMDAR currents (Figure 2C–D; ifenprodil % change: −43.31 ± 16.89, n = 6, p=0.0313; CIQ % change: 86.22 ± 56.54, n = 6, p=0.0313).
evidence: This is inferred from the pharmacological data showing effects of ifenprodil and CIQ but not TCN 201, supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The Ca2+ signal evoked by focal dendritic optogenetic stimulation of PPN axons was not significantly different from the transient evoked by uncaging of RuBi-glutamate in the same dendritic region.
source: The Ca2+ signal evoked by these two stimuli were not significantly different (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by the calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2E-G.

claim: Photo-stimulation of proximal dendrites (within ~70 μm of the soma) reliably evoked responses from PPN ChR2-expressing terminals, whereas photo-stimulation of more distal dendrites almost always failed to evoke a response.
source: In these experiments, photo-stimulation of proximal dendrites (within ~70 um of the soma) reliably evoked responses from PPN ChR2-expressing terminals, whereas photo-stimulation of more distal dendrites almost always failed to evoke a response (Figure 3A,E).
evidence: This is supported by the sCRACM mapping data shown in Figure 3A and 3E.

claim: STN synapses were found in both proximal and distal dendrites of SNc DA neurons.
source: In contrast to PPN synapses, STN synapses were found in both proximal and distal dendrites (Figure 3C,E).
evidence: This is supported by the sCRACM mapping data shown in Figure 3C and 3E.

claim: Uncaging of RuBi-glutamate evoked robust responses in both proximal and distal dendrites of SNc DA neurons.
source: Next, RuBi-glutamate was uncaged (single-photon photolysis) along the dendrite using a focused laser (473 nm) spot. Robust responses were evoked in both proximal and distal dendrites (Figure 3D,E), arguing that there was a relatively uniform distribution of glutamatergic synapses throughout the SNc dendritic tree, in agreement with previous anatomical work (Henny et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the RuBi-glutamate uncaging data shown in Figure 3D and 3E, and citation to Henny et al. (2012).

claim: There is a relatively uniform distribution of glutamatergic synapses throughout the SNc dendritic tree.
source: Robust responses were evoked in both proximal and distal dendrites (Figure 3D,E), arguing that there was a relatively uniform distribution of glutamatergic synapses throughout the SNc dendritic tree, in agreement with previous anatomical work (Henny et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the RuBi-glutamate uncaging data and supported by citation to Henny et al. (2012).

claim: The apparent preferential localization of PPN synapses on proximal dendrites does not reflect a limitation of the sCRACm approach or the inability to detect activation of glutamatergic synapses at distal dendritic locations.
source: Thus, the apparent preferential localization of PPN synapses on proximal dendrites does not reflect a limitation of the sCRACm approach or the inability to detect activation of glutamatergic synapses at distal dendritic locations.
evidence: This is inferred from the control experiments with STN synapses and RuBi-glutamate uncaging.

claim: Proximal glutamatergic synapses onto SNc dopaminergic neurons are better able to drive spiking than more distal ones.
source: Previous work has shown that proximal glutamatergic synapses onto SNc dopaminergic neurons are better able to drive spiking than more distal ones (Blythe et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Blythe et al. (2009).

claim: The probability of evoking a spike in an SNc DA neuron rose rapidly with stimulus intensity.
source: The probability of evoking a spike in an SNc DA neuron rose rapidly with stimulus intensity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Optical stimulation of PPN axons reliably evoked spikes throughout the stimulus train, regardless of the protocol used.
source: Regardless of the protocol used, optical stimulation of PPN axons reliably evoked spikes throughout the stimulus train (Figure 4A–B), with the average spike frequency within the stimulus period being linearly related (with a slope of 1) to the stimulus frequency (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: The average spike frequency within the stimulus period was linearly related (with a slope of 1) to the stimulus frequency.
source: Regardless of the protocol used, optical stimulation of PPN axons reliably evoked spikes throughout the stimulus train (Figure 4A–B), with the average spike frequency within the stimulus period being linearly related (with a slope of 1) to the stimulus frequency (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Application of the NMDAR antagonist CPP did not significantly alter the response to PPN stimulation at any frequency.
source: Surprisingly, application of the NMDAR antagonist CPP, did not significantly alter the response to PPN stimulation at any frequency (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is supported by the pharmacological data shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: Application of the AMPAR antagonist NBQX completely abolished responses to PPN stimulation.
source: In contrast, application of the AMPAR antagonist NBQX completely abolished responses (Figure 4D–F), indicating a dependence on AMPARs, but not NMDARs.
evidence: This is supported by the pharmacological data shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: PPN-evoked burst spiking is dependent on AMPARs, but not NMDARs.
source: In contrast, application of the AMPAR antagonist NBQX completely abolished responses (Figure 4D–F), indicating a dependence on AMPARs, but not NMDARs.
evidence: This is inferred from the pharmacological data showing NBQX abolished responses while CPP did not.

claim: PPN-evoked spikes were frequently truncated in amplitude and had a more hyperpolarized threshold than spikes that were spontaneously generated.
source: Frequently, PPN-evoked spikes were truncated in amplitude and had a more hyperpolarized threshold than spikes that were spontaneously generated (e.g., Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: PPN-evoked truncated spikes likely represent axon initial segment (AIS) spikes that failed to invade the somato-dendritic (SD) region.
source: These likely represent axon initial segment (AIS) spikes that failed to invade the somato-dendritic (SD) region where the electrode was positioned (Grace and Bunney, 1980, 1983a, 1983b).
evidence: This is an inference based on the spike characteristics and supported by citations to Grace and Bunney (1980, 1983a, 1983b).

claim: Antidromically-evoked AIS spikes often fail to generate full SD spikes in SNc DA neurons.
source: Indeed, previous work has shown that antidromically-evoked AIS spikes often fail to generate full SD spikes in SNc DA neurons (Grace and Bunney, 1983b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grace and Bunney (1983b).

claim: When the stimulus occurred towards the end of normal pacemaking cycle, the evoked spikes were indistinguishable from spontaneously occurring spikes.
source: When the stimulus occurred towards the end of normal pacemaking cycle, the evoked spikes were indistinguishable from spontaneously occurring spikes (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: When spikes were evoked early in the oscillation, just after a spontaneously occurring spike, they exhibit more hyperpolarized spike thresholds and reduced amplitudes.
source: In contrast, when spikes were evoked early in the oscillation, just after a spontaneously occurring spike, they exhibit more hyperpolarized spike thresholds and reduced amplitudes, as evident in plots of the first derivative of membrane voltage (dV/dt) as a function of membrane voltage (mV) (Figure 5A,C).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5A and 5C.

claim: PPN-evoked spikes reset the pacemaking cycle.
source: Also, in agreement with previous work (Guzman et al., 2009), PPN-evoked spikes reset the pacemaking cycle, as indicated by a clustering of points around one when comparing the ISI between the evoked spike and the next spontaneously occurring spike to the mean ISI for the cell (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5F and citation to Guzman et al. (2009).

claim: Blocking SK channels with apamin increased the ability of PPN terminals expressing ChR2 to evoke faithful, repetitive (10 Hz) spiking at low stimulus intensities.
source: Indeed, in addition to accelerating pacemaking rate, blocking SK channels with apamin increased the ability of PPN terminals expressing ChR2 to evoke faithful, repetitive (10 Hz) spiking at low stimulus intensities (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: PPN stimulation in the presence of apamin delayed the next spontaneously occurring spike, rather than simply resetting the pacemaking rhythm.
source: Interestingly, PPN stimulation in the presence of apamin delayed the next spontaneously occurring spike, rather than simply resetting the pacemaking rhythm (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The AIS typically arises from a proximal dendrite in SNc DA neurons.
source: As mentioned above, the AIS typically arises from a proximal dendrite in SNc DA neurons (Blythe et al., 2009; Matsuda et al., 2009), in the region where PPN synapses were found.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Blythe et al. (2009) and Matsuda et al. (2009).

claim: PPN-evoked spikes were invariably seen in the axon, regardless of the phase of the pacemaking cycle and the somatic appearance of the spike.
source: More importantly, PPN-evoked spikes were also invariably seen in the axon, regardless of the phase of the pacemaking cycle and the somatic appearance of the spike (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: This is supported by the paired recording data shown in Figure 6B-C.

claim: All somatic spikes showed corresponding axonal spikes, with no failures of somatically recorded spikes to invade the axon.
source: Failure of the somatically recorded spikes to invade the axon would lead to points below the linear trend line, but this was not seen as all somatic spikes showed corresponding axonal spikes (Figure 6D–E).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 6D-E.

claim: AIS spikes alone are capable of triggering axonal firing.
source: This finding is in agreement with previous work showing that AIS spikes alone are capable of triggering axonal firing (Grace and Bunney, 1983b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grace and Bunney (1983b).

claim: There appear to be two general mechanisms by which spike bursts can be generated in SNc DA neurons.
source: Thus, there appear to be two general mechanisms by which spike bursts can be generated in SNc DA neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing both AMPAR-dependent and NMDAR-dependent burst generation mechanisms.

claim: Local application of glutamate can evoke bursts that depend upon activation of NMDARs.
source: In contrast to the PPN-driven mechanism, previous studies have shown that local application of glutamate can evoke bursts that depend upon activation of NMDARs (Johnson and Wu, 2004; Deister et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Johnson and Wu (2004) and Deister et al. (2009).

claim: SNc DA neuron burst spiking can be attenuated by NMDAR antagonists in vivo.
source: In vivo, SNc DA neuron burst spiking can be attenuated by NMDAR antagonists (Charlety et al., 1991; Overton and Clark, 1992; Smith and Grace, 1992; Chergui et al., 1993) or genetic deletion of NMDARs (Zweifel et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple in vivo studies.

claim: Stimulation of the STN in vivo increases burst firing in SNc DA in an NMDA-dependent manner.
source: Similarly, stimulation of the STN in vivo increases burst firing in SNc DA in an NMDA-dependent (Smith and Grace, 1992; Chergui et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Smith and Grace (1992) and Chergui et al. (1994).

claim: NMDAR-dependent bursts harness the intrinsic oscillatory mechanisms of dendrites.
source: The bursts generated in this way harness the intrinsic oscillatory mechanisms of dendrites (Deister et al., 2009; Kuznetsova et al., 2010; Ha and Kuznetsov, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Deister et al. (2009), Kuznetsova et al. (2010), and Ha and Kuznetsov (2013).

claim: Removal of NMDAR voltage sensitivity associated with Mg2+ block abolished burst firing.
source: Using the dynamic clamp technique, Deister et al. (2009) showed that removal of NMDAR voltage sensitivity associated with Mg2+ block abolished burst firing.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Deister et al. (2009).

claim: Tri-heteromeric GluN1-GluN2B-GluN2D NMDARs found at PPN synapses have lower Mg2+ sensitivity.
source: Given that tri-heteromeric GluN1-GluN2B-GluN2D NMDARs found at PPN synapses have lower Mg2+ sensitivity (Huang and Gibb, 2014), it could be that more distally located NMDARs have a different subunit composition that enhance their ability to promote bursts.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Huang and Gibb (2014).

claim: Stimulation of the PPN in vivo produces a significant increase in bursting in ventral tegmental area (VTA) DA neurons and dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens.
source: For example, stimulation of the PPN in vivo produces a significant increase in bursting in ventral tegmental area (VTA) DA neurons and dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens (Floresco et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Floresco et al. (2003).

claim: Lesioning the PPN disrupts dopamine-dependent learning in a variety of behavioral tasks.
source: Moreover, lesioning the PPN disrupts dopamine-dependent learning in a variety of behavioral tasks (Inglis et al., 2000; Alderson et al., 2008; Bortolanza et al., 2010; Jimenez-Martin et al., 2015; Syed et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple behavioral studies.

claim: PPN neurons code for predicted reward value, reward magnitude and stimulus salience.
source: Recordings in behaving animals have shown that PPN neurons code for predicted reward value, reward magnitude and stimulus salience (Pan and Hyland, 2005; Kobayashi and Okada, 2007; Okada et al., 2009; Norton et al., 2011; Okada and Kobayashi, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple in vivo recording studies.

claim: The activity in PPN often precedes that in SNc.
source: Often, the activity in PPN precedes that in SNc (Pan and Hyland, 2005; Kobayashi and Okada, 2007; Okada et al., 2009), raising the possibility that signals from the PPN are critical for the computations performed by DA neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citations to in vivo recording studies.

claim: PPN glutamatergic neurons are implicated in the control of movement gated by the striatum.
source: In addition to reward signaling, recent work has implicated PPN glutamatergic neurons in the control of movement gated by the striatum (Roseberry et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Roseberry et al. (2016).

claim: Phasic activity in SNc DA neurons is temporally correlated not only with the outcomes of actions, but action itself.
source: This inference is consistent with the observation that phasic activity in SNc DA neurons is temporally correlated not only with the outcomes of actions, but action itself (Howe and Dombeck, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Howe and Dombeck (2016).

claim: Glutamatergic innervation of the SNc by the PPN was found to preferentially target proximal regions of the SNc dendritic tree, near where the AIS of these cells generally originates.
source: Glutamatergic innervation of the SNc by the PPN was found to preferentially target proximal regions of the SNc dendritic tree, near where the AIS of these cells generally originates, placing these synapses in a favorable location to drive spiking.
evidence: This summarizes the experimental findings from the sCRACM mapping experiments.

claim: Activation of PPN fibers was capable of directly patterning SNc neuron spiking independently of regular pacemaking activity and without the need to engage NMDARs.
source: In contrast to the previously described mechanism involving the cooperation of intrinsic oscillatory activity with NMDAR activation to generate bursts in SNc neurons, activation of PPN fibers was capable of directly patterning SNc neuron spiking independently of regular pacemaking activity and without the need to engage NMDARs.
evidence: This summarizes the key experimental findings from the pharmacological and stimulation experiments.

claim: The PPN is a likely source of extrinsic control of SNc neuron firing during goal-directed behavior.
source: Nevertheless, this work indicates the PPN is a likely source of extrinsic control of SNc neuron firing during goal-directed behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and their implications.

claim: Male and female C57Bl/6J or DAT-Cre/Ai14-tdTomato mice were used in the experiments.
source: Male and female C57Bl/6J (Jackson Laboratory, Bar Harbor, ME, Stock #000664) or DAT-Cre/Ai14-tdTomato (on a C57Bl/6J background) mice were used.
evidence: This describes the animal models used in the study.

claim: All experiments were performed in accordance with protocols reviewed and approved by the Northwestern Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee and NIH guidelines.
source: All experiments were performed in accordance with protocols reviewed and approved by the Northwestern Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee and NIH guidelines.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance.

claim: Stereotaxic injections were performed when animals were between P16 and P25 days old.
source: Stereotaxic injections were performed when animals were between P16 and P25 days old.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Animals were sacrificed 10–20 days post injection.
source: Animals were sacrificed 10–20 days post injection.
evidence: This describes the experimental timeline.

claim: SNc neurons were identified in coronal or parasagittal ex vivo brain slices based on their morphology, location within the slice, and regular pacemaking activity.
source: SNc neurons were identified in coronal or parasagittal ex vivo brain slices based on their morphology, location within the slice, and regular pacemaking activity (Lacey et al., 1989; Mercuri et al., 1994; Chan et al., 2007; Guzman et al., 2009).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure and is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Glutamatergic responses were isolated by antagonizing GABAA (10 µM gabazine) and nicotinic cholinergic receptors (10 µM mecamylamine).
source: Glutamatergic responses were isolated by antagonizing GABAA (10 µM gabazine) and nicotinic cholinergic receptors (10 µM mecamylamine).

claim: The majority of AMPARs in the brain contain edited GluA2 subunits, making them essentially impermeable to Ca2+.
source: The majority of AMPARs in the brain contain edited GluA2 subunits, making them essentially impermeable to Ca2+ (Kawahara et al., 2003; Wright and Vissel, 2012; Henley and Wilkinson, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: AMPARs lacking edited GluA2 subunits rectify at depolarized membrane potentials.
source: In contrast to AMPARs lacking edited GluA2 subunits, these AMPARs do not rectify at depolarized membrane potentials (Koike et al., 1997; Washburn et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Koike et al. (1997) and Washburn et al. (1997).

claim: NMDARs are obligate heteromers composed of two GluN1 and two GluN2 subunits.
source: NMDARs are obligate heteromers composed of two GluN1 and two GluN2 subunits.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NMDAR structure.

claim: The identity of the two GluN2 subunits significantly impacts properties of the receptor, such as sensitivity to Mg2+ block and relative Ca2+ permeability.
source: The identity of the two GluN2 subunits significantly impacts properties of the receptor, such as sensitivity to Mg2+ block and relative Ca2+ permeability.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NMDAR function.

claim: The majority of NMDARs in the brain contain a combination of GluN2A and GluN2B subunits.
source: While the majority of NMDARs in the brain contain a combination of GluN2A and GluN2B subunits (Monyer et al., 1994; Wyllie et al., 2013), previous work has shown that NMDARs in SNc DA neurons contain GluN2B and GluN2D subunits (Jones and Gibb, 2005; Brothwell et al., 2008; Suárez et al., 2010; Huang and Gibb, 2014), with the latter conferring reduced Mg2+ sensitivity and Ca2+ permeability (Siegler Retchless et al., 2012; Huang and Gibb, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Previous work has shown that NMDARs in SNc DA neurons contain GluN2B and GluN2D subunits.
source: While the majority of NMDARs in the brain contain a combination of GluN2A and GluN2B subunits (Monyer et al., 1994; Wyllie et al., 2013), previous work has shown that NMDARs in SNc DA neurons contain GluN2B and GluN2D subunits (Jones and Gibb, 2005; Brothwell et al., 2008; Suárez et al., 2010; Huang and Gibb, 2014), with the latter conferring reduced Mg2+ sensitivity and Ca2+ permeability (Siegler Retchless et al., 2012; Huang and Gibb, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: GluN2D subunits confer reduced Mg2+ sensitivity and Ca2+ permeability to NMDARs.
source: While the majority of NMDARs in the brain contain a combination of GluN2A and GluN2B subunits (Monyer et al., 1994; Wyllie et al., 2013), previous work has shown that NMDARs in SNc DA neurons contain GluN2B and GluN2D subunits (Jones and Gibb, 2005; Brothwell et al., 2008; Suárez et al., 2010; Huang and Gibb, 2014), with the latter conferring reduced Mg2+ sensitivity and Ca2+ permeability (Siegler Retchless et al., 2012; Huang and Gibb, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Siegler Retchless et al. (2012) and Huang and Gibb (2014).

claim: The positioning of PPN glutamatergic synapses on proximal dendrites near the AIS should maximize their ability to control spike generation.
source: The positioning of PPN glutamatergic synapses on proximal dendrites near the AIS should maximize their ability to control spike generation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical location of the synapses and established principles of neuronal excitability.

claim: The AIS origin of the PPN evoked spikes was consistent with the dependence of the nominal spike threshold and amplitude on the phase of the pacemaking cycle and the faithful propagation of evoked spikes down the axon.
source: The AIS origin of the PPN evoked spikes was consistent with several features of the somatic recordings, including the dependence of the nominal spike threshold and amplitude on the phase of the pacemaking cycle and the faithful propagation of evoked spikes down the axon.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from multiple experimental observations.

claim: The degree of PPN convergence on individual SNc DA neurons is uncertain.
source: The degree of PPN convergence on individual SNc DA neurons also is uncertain.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation artificially synchronizes spiking in PPN axons, producing a temporal summation of synaptic inputs that may not occur in vivo.
source: Optogenetic stimulation artificially synchronizes spiking in PPN axons, producing a temporal summation of synaptic inputs that may not occur in vivo.

claim: The steep relationship between optical stimulus intensity and SNc DA neuron spike probability is consistent with the possibility that individual SNc DA neurons are innervated by a small number of PPN axons.
source: The steep relationship between optical stimulus intensity and SNc DA neuron spike probability is consistent with this possibility.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: A sparse mapping between PPN and SNc would provide an explanation for the variability in SNc burst patterns observed in vivo.
source: This kind of mapping between PPN and SNc would provide an explanation for the variability in SNc burst patterns observed in vivo (Grace and Bunney, 1984b; Hyland et al., 2002).
evidence: This is speculation about the functional implications of the findings, supported by citations to in vivo observations.

claim: PPN glutamatergic synapses are capable of determining the precise timing of SNc DA neuron spikes that are propagated down the axon to target structures, like the striatum.
source: Regardless, these experiments demonstrate that PPN glutamatergic synapses are capable of determining the precise timing of SNc DA neuron spikes that are propagated down the axon to target structures, like the striatum.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: PPN synapses were capable of driving precisely structured bursts, like those recorded in vivo.
source: Moreover, PPN synapses were capable of driving precisely structured bursts, like those recorded in vivo (Grace and Bunney, 1984b).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data and citation to in vivo recordings.

claim: Focal application of glutamate to proximal dendrites and local electrical stimulation of glutamatergic axons are capable of producing spike bursts.
source: This result is consistent with previous studies showing that focal application of glutamate to proximal dendrites, as well as local electrical stimulation of glutamatergic axons, was capable of producing spike bursts (Blythe et al., 2007, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The dependence of NMDAR-dependent bursts upon intrinsic oscillatory mechanisms will allow pacemaking and ongoing synaptic input to influence the timing of bursts.
source: The dependence upon intrinsic oscillatory mechanisms will undoubtedly allow pacemaking and ongoing synaptic input, particularly GABAergic synaptic activity, to influence the timing of bursts, contrasting it with the 'short-circuiting' of these processes by PPN synapses.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional differences between the two burst generation mechanisms.

claim: PPN synapses 'short-circuit' the influence of pacemaking and ongoing synaptic input on burst timing.
source: The dependence upon intrinsic oscillatory mechanisms will undoubtedly allow pacemaking and ongoing synaptic input, particularly GABAergic synaptic activity, to influence the timing of bursts, contrasting it with the 'short-circuiting' of these processes by PPN synapses.
evidence: This is an inference about how PPN synapses differ from NMDAR-dependent mechanisms.

claim: NMDAR-dependent burst generation depends upon the voltage-dependence of Mg2+ block.
source: Another interesting feature of the NMDAR-dependent burst is its dependence upon the voltage-dependence of Mg2+ block.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Deister et al. (2009).

claim: More distally located NMDARs may have a different subunit composition that enhances their ability to promote bursts.
source: Given that tri-heteromeric GluN1-GluN2B-GluN2D NMDARs found at PPN synapses have lower Mg2+ sensitivity (Huang and Gibb, 2014), it could be that more distally located NMDARs have a different subunit composition that enhance their ability to promote bursts.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known properties of different NMDAR subtypes.

claim: The differential engagement of synaptic and extrasynaptic NMDARs by the two different modes of burst generation could have important long-term consequences.
source: Given the differences in postsynaptic signaling by synaptic and extrasynaptic NMDARs (Hardingham and Bading, 2010; Paoletti et al., 2013), the differential engagement by the two different modes of burst generation could have important long-term consequences.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional implications, supported by citations about NMDAR signaling.

claim: Basal ganglia control of PPN glutamatergic neurons may be fed back to the SNc and broadcast to the striatum, allowing complex movement sequences to be executed.
source: Nevertheless, it is tempting to speculate that the basal ganglia control of PPN glutamatergic neurons described by Roseberry et al. (2016) is fed back to the SNc and broadcast to the striatum, allowing complex movement sequences to be executed – a capacity that is lost in PD patients with degeneration of SNc DA neurons (Hernández et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation about the functional implications, supported by citations.
